subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Exam evidence::Paper 3: Crime and deviance with theory and methods::Crime and deviance::4.3.1 (4) Crime control, surveillance, prevention and punishment, victims, and the role of the criminal justice system and other agencies

front: Build an evaluation chain about the relationship between sociological research and social policy.
back:
Model answer

Research can reveal patterns and assess interventions, giving policy makers evidence. However, policy can reflect ideological priorities and select findings that fit them; evidence therefore influences policy but does not determine it. A judgement should consider the issue, evidence quality and political context.

Marking points

  • Explain a route from research to policy
  • Explain how policy priorities shape evidence use
  • Reach a qualified judgement

Common trap

Do not assume research automatically determines government policy.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Theory and methods::Evaluation
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 6-mark “outline three reasons” item asks why policies to raise disadvantaged pupils’ achievement may fail. Give a reusable response plan and one model chain.
back:
Model answer

Offer three different causes and explain the effect of each. For example, pupils may avoid means-tested help because claiming it identifies them as poor, so support fails to reach everyone eligible.

Marking points

  • Identify three distinct reasons
  • Explain how each limits the policy’s impact

Common trap

Do not give three policy names without explaining why they fall short.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Education::Short answer
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Plan a balanced judgement for “Sociology can be scientific.”
back:
Model answer

Argument: systematic measurement and testing can produce reliable evidence. Counterargument: people interpret situations and research can affect behaviour, limiting prediction and objectivity. Judgement: whether Sociology is scientific depends on the definition of science and the research question; methods can be systematic without reproducing natural-science laws.

Marking points

  • Define the criterion for science
  • Develop a supporting argument
  • Develop a relevant challenge
  • Make a conditional, justified judgement

Common trap

Do not present positivism or interpretivism as AQA’s endorsed answer.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Theory and methods::Comparative evaluation
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Mini-scenario: repeated headlines call a group a public threat after a few incidents. Explain one possible crime-amplification chain.
back:
Model answer

Selective headlines can create a moral panic by presenting the group as a threat. Heightened public concern may prompt tougher policing, increasing surveillance and recorded incidents; stigma and conflict may then reinforce deviant identities. This is a possible process, not an inevitable effect.

Marking points

  • Apply scenario detail
  • Explain moral panic or amplification
  • Develop a causal chain and qualify the claim

Common trap

Do not assume that intensified attention proves the original threat was objectively large.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::Media and crime
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Mini-claim: “Official figures prove working-class people commit most crime.” Give a precise sociological correction.
back:
Model answer

Official crime data do not provide one comprehensive offending rate by class. Police-recorded or court data reflect reported offences and justice processing; CSEW socioeconomic measures concern victimisation and are proxies, not class-based offender rates. Marxist and other explanations can be discussed as theories, with evidence limits made explicit.

Marking points

  • Distinguish offending from recorded/processed crime
  • State that an overall class-specific offender rate is not available in these series
  • Distinguish victimisation/socioeconomic proxies from class offending
  • Evaluate claim with a theoretical explanation as an argument, not a measured fact

Common trap

Do not use a working-class share of prison or arrest totals as an offending rate without population denominators and controls.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::Class and crime measurement
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: An item-based question provides a short school or neighbourhood scenario. How should the item be used?
back:
Model answer

Select a specific detail from the item and connect it to a sociological concept; explain how that detail illustrates the mechanism in the question. Add relevant knowledge, then add a distinct point if the question asks for one.

Marking points

  • Specific item detail
  • Explicit application link to concept
  • Sociological explanation that answers the wording

Common trap

Quoting the item without explaining its sociological relevance is not developed application.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::10-mark analyse
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A question says “Outline two ways”. What should each point contain?
back:
Model answer

Give two distinct, relevant ways and briefly explain each. Keep each point accurate and focused on the wording.

Marking points

  • Two distinct relevant points
  • Brief explanation showing how each answers the prompt

Common trap

Two labels with no explanation may not show the required outline.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::4-mark outline
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Prompt: “Recorded offending is higher in group X, so group X commits more crime.” Give a developed challenge.
back:
Model answer

Recorded rates depend on reporting, police visibility and official decisions as well as offending. Compare with victimisation or self-report evidence, while acknowledging that those sources also omit offences and depend on disclosure.

Marking points

  • Distinguish recorded crime from all offending
  • Explain a recording/surveillance mechanism
  • Use a second data source and state its limitation

Common trap

Do not assume a victim survey captures every type of offence.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::Distribution and measurement
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Plan a 30-mark “Evaluate” essay on an explanation of crime. What should the response do?
back:
Model answer

Define the focus, build several developed arguments supporting the view, test them with relevant alternatives and evidence, and make comparative judgements throughout. Conclude by answering “how far” using the strongest criteria.

Marking points

  • Accurate knowledge and concepts
  • Relevant application to the question
  • Developed analysis and evaluation
  • Reasoned judgement across the argument and in the conclusion

Common trap

A memorised theory dump or an unsupported final “it depends” does not evaluate the specific claim.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::30-mark essay
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Put the police, CPS, courts and HMPPS roles into a simple sequence.
back:
Model answer

In a case referred to the CPS, police investigate and gather evidence; the CPS reviews and presents the prosecution; the court decides the case and sentences if appropriate; prison and probation services administer relevant sentences and support rehabilitation. Police may make charging decisions for less serious cases.

Marking points

  • Distinguish investigation, prosecution and court functions
  • Explain the role of prison and probation services after sentencing

Common trap

Do not treat the CPS as the body that decides guilt.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::Criminal justice agencies
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 20-mark Methods in Context question asks students to evaluate a named method for researching a named education issue, using an item. What should each developed paragraph do?
back:
Model answer

Start with one method feature; connect it to the specific school issue and participants; explain its practical, ethical or theoretical consequence for evidence; use the item where relevant; then weigh the consequence or compare a limitation.

Marking points

  • Accurate method knowledge
  • Application to the specified education context and item
  • Analysis/evaluation of evidence consequences

Common trap

The AQA examiner report says general method discussion applied to education in general is weaker than application to the specific issue and group; do not assert every method point is automatically valid or invalid.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Methods in context
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: For a 30-mark “evaluate the view” essay on whether gender differences in subject choice and achievement mainly result from wider society, what makes a developed paragraph?
back:
Model answer

State a focused claim; explain a sociological mechanism; link it to subject choice or achievement; use relevant evidence or concepts; evaluate it with a competing school-based or individual explanation; connect the evaluation to the “mainly” judgement. For 30-mark essays, AQA uses level-based AO1/AO2/AO3 descriptors; conclude by weighing explanations.

Marking points

  • AO1: accurate relevant concepts/evidence
  • AO2: sustained focus on the issue and any supplied item
  • AO3: developed analysis/evaluation and justified judgement

Common trap

A list of theories or an unsupported conclusion does not establish which explanation is more important.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Education::Extended response
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: How can an essay on crime use AQA’s core themes as analytical threads?
back:
Model answer

Connect socialisation, culture and identity to how peer groups, gender identities or labels shape conduct; connect social differentiation, power and stratification to unequal resources, law-making, policing or victimisation. Explain each link to the exact claim in the question.

Marking points

  • Name a relevant core theme
  • Use a specific crime concept/theory
  • Explain the link to the question rather than listing the theme

Common trap

Do not mention “power” or “identity” as a label without explaining its effect on the crime process.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::Paper 3 integration
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A student claims that paid employment has made family relationships equal. Give a developed evaluation using domestic labour and power.
back:
Model answer

Paid work can increase women’s financial independence and bargaining power. However, a second shift may leave women responsible for much unpaid work, so employment alone does not establish equality. Assess equality by considering both labour and control over resources.

Marking points

  • Link paid work to potential economic independence/bargaining power
  • Explain continuing unequal domestic labour as a limit
  • Use the limit to reach a qualified judgement about equality

Common trap

Do not treat paid employment as proof that unpaid work or decision-making is equal.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Families and households::Gender and power
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A question says “Outline three reasons”. What response structure is reliable?
back:
Model answer

State three distinct reasons and add a brief sociological explanation for each. Avoid repeating the same causal idea in different wording.

Marking points

  • Three distinct reasons
  • Each reason is briefly developed and relevant

Common trap

Do not spend most of the answer expanding one reason and leave the other two as labels.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::6-mark outline
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A town’s annual religious festival brings residents together and raises money for shared services. Apply a functionalist explanation of religion to this example.
back:
Model answer

The shared festival is a ritual that can reinforce collective identity and belonging. Fundraising for shared services shows how religious organisation may contribute to practical community cooperation. The explanation is functionalist because it links religion with integration and social solidarity.

Marking points

  • Identify the festival as a shared ritual
  • Apply collective identity/belonging to residents
  • Link community cooperation to integration/solidarity

Common trap

Do not assume a functionalist explanation rules out religious conflict.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Beliefs in society::Religion and social change
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: An exam item says that UK policies protect vulnerable children but also restrict children from paid work. Using the item, analyse two ways policies may have affected children’s status.
back:
Model answer

Protective policies such as safeguarding can recognise children as a group needing special protection, supporting a child-centred view. The item’s age limits on paid work can protect children from exploitation but also restrict economic independence. This applies both parts of the item and explains contrasting effects on status.

Marking points

  • Apply the protection cue to special status/child-centredness
  • Apply employment restrictions to limited economic independence
  • Explain how each policy shapes children’s status

Common trap

Do not assume that restrictions have only benefits or only drawbacks.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Families and households::Childhood
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: Assess the claim that globalisation shows religion is becoming more significant. State one supporting argument, one qualification and a judgement.
back:
Model answer

Global communication and migration can spread religions and enable transnational communities, supporting the claim that religion remains influential. Yet the visibility or spread of religion does not by itself show that overall participation or institutional authority is increasing; secularisation may occur unevenly across societies and dimensions. Globalisation therefore challenges a simple universal decline thesis but does not alone disprove secularisation.

Marking points

  • Explain a mechanism by which globalisation spreads or sustains religion
  • Distinguish visibility/spread from overall religiosity or authority
  • Make a qualified judgement that recognises uneven change

Common trap

Do not assume religious visibility proves religious participation is increasing everywhere.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Beliefs in society::Secularisation
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: How can you compare two sociological explanations rather than write separate theory summaries?
back:
Model answer

Compare their assumptions, the causes each identifies and what each explains well; then judge which account better explains the precise outcome in the question, using evidence and limitations.

Marking points

  • Comparison on a shared issue
  • Evidence or reasoning for each view
  • Explicit judgement about explanatory power

Common trap

Do not describe each theory separately without comparing how they explain the same issue.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::30-mark essay
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A question says “Analyse two ways”. How do you develop each way?
back:
Model answer

Make two distinct analytical points, explain the mechanism linking each to the outcome in the question, and use relevant sociological knowledge or context. A short causal chain makes the link explicit.

Marking points

  • Two distinct ways/reasons
  • Developed explanation of each causal link
  • Relevant concepts or evidence used accurately

Common trap

A list of factors without explaining how they produce the named outcome is descriptive, not developed analysis.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Crime and deviance::10-mark analyse
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 10-mark item asks for two ways feminism may influence research design. What should a focused answer do?
back:
Model answer

First, a feminist researcher might choose unpaid housework as a topic because women’s experiences have been neglected. Second, a researcher seeking a more equal relationship with participants might use open interviews and let them shape the discussion.

Marking points

  • Explain two different links between feminism and research design
  • Relate each to a concrete design choice

Common trap

Do not describe feminism without explaining how it changes the research plan.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Theory and methods
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: An item says pupils from one group outperform another even among pupils receiving free school meals. How should a 10-mark answer explain two reasons?
back:
Model answer

Develop two explanations and explicitly use the item in each. For example, connect the item’s within-FSM comparison to differences in teacher expectations or home support; then explain a mechanism such as expectations shaping grouping and feedback. Add analysis of how the mechanism could produce attainment differences, while avoiding claims that every pupil in a group is alike.

Marking points

  • Accurate knowledge of two relevant explanations
  • Two explicit, developed uses of the item
  • Analysis showing how explanations could produce the pattern

Common trap

Do not switch to explaining a different pattern, such as underachievement, without answering the stated item.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Education::Item application
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 20-mark question asks you to evaluate overt participant observation for researching pupil subcultures in schools. What should a focused response chain do?
back:
Model answer

Participation could let a researcher hear pupils’ informal meanings, improving insight into the group. However, pupils who know an adult is observing may hide rule-breaking; access and consent also need negotiation. Explain how each issue affects the evidence and use relevant details from the item.

Marking points

  • Apply benefits and limitations of observation to the pupils and setting
  • Evaluate consequences for the research evidence

Common trap

Do not list generic method strengths without connecting them to the pupil group.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Methods in context::Observation of pupil subcultures
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 30-mark question asks you to evaluate how useful Marxist perspectives are for understanding education’s role. What argument structure should a strong answer use?
back:
Model answer

Explain relevant Marxist claims (ideology, reproduction and legitimation of class inequality) and apply supplied item material. Evaluate by comparing different Marxist accounts and relevant functionalist, feminist, New Right or interactionist explanations; consider what each explains about education’s role and where it is incomplete. Reach a judgement on usefulness rather than declaring one perspective wholly true or false.

Marking points

  • Use accurate knowledge, relevant application, developed evaluation and a reasoned judgement

Common trap

A descriptive account of Marxism or a bolt-on criticism does not answer “how useful”; compare explanations and judge their reach.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Education::Role and functions
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 4-mark “outline two” item asks for two material factors affecting class achievement. What does a complete response need?
back:
Model answer

Give two different material constraints and explain how each affects learning. For example, a crowded home may leave no quiet place for homework; hunger can make it harder to concentrate in lessons.

Marking points

  • Identify two material factors
  • Link each factor to educational achievement

Common trap

Do not supply two labels without explaining their effects.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Education::Short answer
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: An item says that urban growth weakens local religious communities and that scientific explanations replace some religious accounts. Explain two ways social change may contribute to secularisation. (10-mark Paper 2 format)
back:
Model answer

Urbanisation can weaken close-knit communities that once reinforced shared religious practice, reducing the social support for participation. The growth of scientific and technical explanations can also make religious accounts less influential in some areas of life. Both links describe possible mechanisms; neither establishes that religion declines in every society or dimension.

Marking points

  • Explain social change through urbanisation and connect it to weaker community-based practice
  • Explain growth of scientific/technical explanations and connect it to reduced religious authority in some areas
  • Develop each chain rather than merely naming changes
  • Keep the claim bounded rather than asserting universal decline

Common trap

Do not list changes such as urbanisation or science without explaining their possible effect on belief or practice.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Beliefs in society::Secularisation
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: A 10-mark “outline and explain two” Theory and Methods item asks for two ways a theoretical perspective affects research. What is a complete explanation?
back:
Model answer

For each way, state a theoretical assumption, identify the method or evidence it favours, and explain why that method fits the assumption. Example: interpretivists prioritise actors’ meanings, so flexible interviews can reveal how participants define a situation.

Marking points

  • Two distinct theoretical-method links
  • Each link explains the reasoning, not just labels

Common trap

Do not replace explanation of the theory-method link with an unrelated evaluation of the theory.
subdeck_path: AQA A-level Sociology 7192 – Mark Scheme::Theory and methods
paper: Assessment skills

point.title: Exam technique

front: An item says that more people live alone or cohabit than in the past, while the married nuclear family remains common. Using the item and your knowledge, evaluate sociological explanations of family diversity. (20-mark Paper 2 format)
back:
Model answer

The item suggests both greater diversity and continued importance of the married family. Postmodern and personal-life approaches explain varied pathways through greater choice and negotiated relationships; lone-parent, reconstituted and living-apart-together arrangements illustrate different structures. However, choices are shaped by resources, gender relations and policy, so diversity should not be reduced to free individual choice. Chester’s neo-conventional argument also cautions that the nuclear family remains significant, while that does not make it the only form or show that it best serves everyone. Overall, family life is diverse in structure and pathway, but its extent depends on the measure and social group considered.

Marking points

  • Apply both sides of the item: diversity and continued prevalence of marriage
  • Explain relevant perspectives and examples of varied family forms
  • Develop evaluation of individual choice and structural constraints
  • Reach a qualified conclusion about extent and measurement

Common trap

Avoid treating the presence of more forms as proof that the nuclear family has disappeared, or treating prevalence as proof it is universal.
